lead: This unit shows how a computer recovers the structure of a sentence: which words group together, which word depends on which, and which parse a human would prefer. After working through it you can write a small grammar, convert it to normal form, trace CYK and Earley by hand, score trees with a PCFG, draw a dependency tree, tag chunks, and run a shift-reduce parse step by step.
about: This unit is about syntax and parsing. Chapter 3.1 sets up context-free grammars and the phrase-structure rules of English. Chapter 3.2 turns those rules into parser-ready normal form and grounds them in treebank data. Chapter 3.3 gives the two workhorse algorithms, CYK and Earley. Chapter 3.4 shows why one sentence gets many trees and how the right one is chosen. Chapter 3.5 makes that choice statistical with PCFGs, and chapter 3.8 adds head words and a left-to-right shift-reduce search. Chapter 3.6 moves from phrases to word-to-word links, and chapter 3.7 stops at flat chunks when a full parse is not needed. Each chapter ends with a measure or a trace you can compute by hand.

chapters.idea: A context-free grammar is a small set of rewrite rules that generates infinitely many sentences, and English phrase structure can be written as such rules.
chapters.depth: Define the grammar as a 4-tuple (N nonterminals, Σ terminals, R rules, S start symbol) and define terminal, nonterminal, derivation, leftmost derivation, parse tree, yield, generation and recognition. Give the standard English rule set: S → NP VP, NP → Det N, NP → NP PP, VP → V NP, VP → VP PP, PP → P NP, plus lexical rules such as N → boy. Show that recursion makes a finite grammar cover unbounded sentences. One line on the Chomsky hierarchy placing CFG above regular grammar. Some syllabi call these phrase-structure rules or PSG. Close with feature structures and unification: attribute-value matrices, the unification operation, and how [NUM sg] on NP and VP blocks 'the boys eats'. Only a few universities teach feature structures, so keep it to one short section.

figure.aria: A parse tree for the sentence the boy ate the cake, with S at the root, NP and VP below it, and the words at the leaves.

chapters.example: Grammar G: S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; Det → the | a; N → boy | cake | girl; V → ate | saw. (a) Give the leftmost derivation and the parse tree of 'the boy ate a cake'. (b) How many sentences does G generate? Answer: (a) S ⇒ NP VP ⇒ Det N VP ⇒ the N VP ⇒ the boy VP ⇒ the boy V NP ⇒ the boy ate NP ⇒ the boy ate Det N ⇒ the boy ate a N ⇒ the boy ate a cake. (b) NP = 2 Det × 3 N = 6 strings; VP = 2 V × 6 NP = 12; S = 6 × 12 = 72 sentences.
chapters.trap: Writing a terminal such as 'boy' as if it were a nonterminal, and claiming a CFG can enforce agreement or match nested brackets. Also mixing up the start symbol with the first rule written.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (morphology, word classes) and Unit 2 (POS tags such as Det, N, V).
chapters.leave: Probabilities to 3.5, parsing algorithms to 3.3, rule counts from corpora to 3.2, meaning and selectional restrictions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A treebank supplies real annotated trees, and Chomsky normal form rewrites any CFG into binary rules that a parser can use.
chapters.depth: Define a treebank as a corpus of sentences with their syntactic annotation; mention bracketed constituency treebanks and dependency treebanks, POS tags plus phrase labels, and head marking. Show how rules and their counts are read off a treebank (grammar induction from data), and note sparse or unseen rules in one line. Then define Chomsky normal form: every rule is A → BC with B and C nonterminals, or A → a with a single terminal. Give the three conversion steps: isolate a terminal that sits beside nonterminals (VP → V NP becomes VP → V1 NP, V1 → V), binarise right-hand sides longer than two with new nonterminals, then remove unit and ε rules and re-add what the start symbol needs. State that the language is unchanged and grammar size grows only linearly. Name Greibach normal form only. Some syllabi call this CNF or Chomsky Normal Form.

figure.title: Rewriting a rule into CNF
figure.aria: A four-step flow that splits a three-symbol rule into two binary rules and isolates a terminal, ending in a CNF grammar.

chapters.example: Convert this grammar to CNF and give the rule count: S → NP VP PP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; PP → P NP; Det → the | a; N → boy | girl; V → ate; P → with. Answer: S is three symbols long, so add X1 → VP PP and rewrite S → NP X1. Every other structural rule already has two symbols. No rule mixes a terminal with nonterminals, because the words sit in separate lexical rules. The CNF grammar is S → NP X1, X1 → VP PP, NP → Det N, VP → V NP, PP → P NP, Det → the, Det → a, N → boy, N → girl, V → ate, P → with: 11 rules against 10 before, and it generates exactly the same sentences.
chapters.trap: Binarising left instead of right in a way that changes the yield, or forgetting to restore a unit rule for the start symbol after deleting unit rules. CNF never changes the language, only the shape of the rules.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for rules, derivations and parse trees.
chapters.leave: Probabilities estimated from the treebank to 3.5, dependency treebanks and head rules to 3.6.

chapters.idea: CYK fills a table of spans bottom-up for a CNF grammar, and Earley reads the sentence left to right with dotted rules, so both find every parse without blind search.
chapters.depth: Start with parsing as recognition plus tree output, and one line each on top-down parsing (recursive descent, loops on left recursion), bottom-up parsing and chart parsing, which some syllabi list as 'theories of parsing'. CYK: a triangular table of n(n+1)/2 cells, cell (i, j) holding the set of nonterminals that span words i to j; fill the length-1 cells from lexical rules; for each longer span try every split k and add A when B is in (i, k), C is in (k+1, j) and A → BC exists; complexity O(n³·|G|); CNF is required. Earley: a state is a rule with a dot and an origin position; the three operations PREDICTOR, SCANNER and COMPLETER; one chart set per word position; O(n³) in general, O(n²) for an unambiguous grammar and O(n) for bounded-state grammars; it accepts any CFG including left recursion and ε rules.

figure.title: CYK table, 'the boy ate the cake'
figure.aria: A triangular CYK table where the cell for words 1 to 5 contains S, so the sentence is accepted.

chapters.example: Grammar in CNF: S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; Det → the; N → boy | cake; V → ate. Run CYK on 'the boy ate the cake' (words 1 to 5) and say if it is accepted. Answer: length 1 gives [1,1]=Det, [2,2]=N, [3,3]=V, [4,4]=Det, [5,5]=N. Length 2: [1,2]=NP from Det N, [4,5]=NP, and [2,3]=[3,4]=empty. Length 3: [3,5]=VP from V and [4,5]=NP; [1,3]=[2,4]=empty. Length 4: [1,4]=[2,5]=empty. Length 5: split at k=2 gives NP in [1,2] and VP in [3,5], so S is in [1,5] and the sentence is accepted. The number of split checks is 4 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 20.
chapters.trap: Running CYK on a grammar that is not in CNF, or reading cell (i, j) as words i to j-1. In Earley the three operations are steps taken in order as the dot moves, not three alternative algorithms.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2, especially CNF and parse trees.
chapters.leave: Probabilities inside the CYK table to 3.5, dependency parsing algorithms to 3.6, chunk tagging to 3.7.

chapters.idea: One string can have many parse trees, and choosing among them needs evidence beyond the grammar: probabilities, head words and word meaning.
chapters.depth: Separate structural ambiguity from lexical ambiguity. Cover the standard patterns: prepositional-phrase attachment ('I saw the man with the telescope'), coordination scope ('old men and women'), noun-noun compounds, and garden-path sentences ('The horse raced past the barn fell'). Distinguish local ambiguity (one rule, two possible trees) from global ambiguity, and say that the number of parses rises quickly as phrases are added. List the evidence used to resolve attachment: PCFG probability (3.5), head words (3.8), selectional restrictions and word senses (Unit 4), and the heuristics of low attachment and minimal attachment, with a line on why each fails. Mention that practical parsers keep n-best parses and rerank them.

figure.title: Resolving a PP attachment
figure.aria: One ambiguous sentence branches into two parses, which are scored, checked against word evidence, and reduced to one chosen tree.

nodes.label: Sentence
nodes.note: I saw the man with the telescope

chapters.example: 'I saw the man with the telescope'. Write both bracketings, name the reading each gives, and choose one with P(VP → VP PP) = 0.6 and P(NP → NP PP) = 0.2 when all other rules are shared. Answer: Parse A is [VP saw [NP the man [PP with the telescope]]], where the man has the telescope, giving NP = 0.2 times the shared factor. Parse B is [VP saw [NP the man] [PP with the telescope]], where the seeing is done with the telescope, giving VP = 0.6 times the same shared factor. Parse B wins, 0.6 against 0.2, which agrees with the low-attachment guess here.
chapters.trap: Calling a word with two senses structurally ambiguous, or assuming the highest-probability tree is the correct meaning. Low attachment and minimal attachment are heuristics and each one fails on some ordinary sentence.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for trees and 3.3 for how a parser returns more than one tree.
chapters.leave: Rule probability detail to 3.5, head-word conditioning to 3.8, word senses and selectional restrictions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A PCFG puts a probability on every rule, so the probability of a tree is the product of its rule probabilities and the best tree can be found by dynamic programming.
chapters.depth: Define a PCFG as a CFG plus a probability for each rule, with the probabilities of all rules sharing a left-hand side summing to 1. Give the tree probability as the product of the rules used, and state the independence assumptions: a rule's children are independent given the parent, with no head word and no outside context. Define inside probability β(i, j, A) as the summed probability of all subtrees rooted at A over words i to j. Give probabilistic CYK: the same table as 3.3, using max for the most likely tree (Viterbi style) and sum for the sentence probability. Quote complexity O(n³·|G|). Estimating rule probabilities from a treebank by relative frequency, the sparse-data problem, and one line on smoothing (Unit 2). List the limitations: bias toward small trees, no lexical sensitivity, weak on attachment. Name evaluation with labelled precision, recall and F1 over constituents. Parent annotation and Markovisation named only.

figure.aria: A parse tree for the boy ate the cake with each rule probability on its edge; the product along the tree is 0.0036.

chapters.example: For 'the boy ate the cake' take P(S → NP VP) = 1.0, P(NP → Det N) = 0.5, P(VP → V NP) = 0.6, P(Det → the) = 1.0, P(N → boy) = 0.3, P(N → cake) = 0.2, P(V → ate) = 0.4. Find the tree probability and the sentence probability. Answer: the tree uses nine rules, so multiply 1.0 × 0.5 × 1.0 × 0.3 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.5 × 1.0 × 0.2 = 0.0036. This grammar gives the sentence only one tree, so the sentence probability is also 0.0036; with several trees you would add their probabilities instead.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that a rule is counted once for every node that uses it, and using rule probabilities that do not sum to 1 across the right-hand sides of the same left-hand symbol. The max in the table is the best tree, not the sentence probability.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for rules, 3.2 for treebank counts, 3.3 for the CYK table.
chapters.leave: Smoothing methods to Unit 2, lexical heads to 3.8, semantic scoring to Unit 4, neural parsers to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Dependency grammar describes a sentence as words linked head to dependent with labels, and dependency parsing finds the best such tree.
chapters.depth: Define head, dependent, root, and the link labels (nsubj, dobj, det, amod, advmod, and a preposition link). Give the tree constraints: every word has exactly one head, one word links to ROOT, no cycles, all words connected. Explain projectivity and crossing arcs, and why dependency suits freer word order languages such as Hindi and Tamil. Transition-based arc-standard parsing: a stack, a buffer, and the actions LEFT-ARC, RIGHT-ARC, SHIFT, driven by a classifier or an oracle. One line on graph-based parsing that maximises total arc score over all trees, naming the Chu-Liu/Edmonds algorithm. Give UAS and LAS with the counting convention. One short paragraph on a neural shift-reduce dependency parser that scores the moves from the top stack words and the next word: only a few universities go this deep.

figure.aria: A dependency tree for the boy ate the cake, with ate as the root, boy as its subject, cake as its object and the two determiners hanging from their nouns.

chapters.example: Gold dependency tree for 'The boy ate the cake quickly': ate→boy nsubj, boy→The det, ate→cake dobj, cake→the det, ate→quickly advmod, ate→ROOT. A system outputs everything correctly except that it links cake→quickly advmod. Find UAS and LAS, counting every arc including the one from ate to ROOT. Answer: there are 6 arcs. Unlabelled, 5 arcs have the right head and dependent, so UAS = 5/6 = 0.833. Labelled, the same 5 also carry the right label, so LAS = 5/6 = 0.833.
chapters.trap: Dropping the ROOT arc from the denominator, or counting words instead of arcs. Arcs must form a tree: a word with two heads or a cycle is invalid even if each arc looks plausible.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for constituency as a contrast, Unit 2 for POS tags that the parser reads.
chapters.leave: Named entity recognition to Unit 2, semantic roles and selectional restrictions to Unit 4, neural encoders to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Shallow parsing groups words into flat chunks without internal structure, which is cheap and enough for many tasks.
chapters.depth: Define a chunk as a non-overlapping, non-nesting group such as a base noun phrase, and say what is left unchunked. Give the IOB scheme (B-, I-, O, and BILOU by name) and show chunking as sequence labelling over the POS tags, so an HMM, MEMM or CRF from Unit 2 can be reused. One line on rule-based chunking with patterns over tags such as Det? Adj* N+ and on the idea of chinks. Give chunk-level precision, recall and F1, stressing exact boundary and label match, and distinguish labelled from unlabelled scores. Give uses: named entity recognition, information extraction, fast partial parsing, and fallback when a full parser fails.

figure.title: Chunks as IOB tags
figure.aria: Three rows lining up the words, their POS tags and the IOB chunk tags, with each noun phrase marked B-NP then I-NP.

chapters.example: For 'The boy ate the cake in the park' the gold chunks are [The boy]NP, [ate]VP, [the cake]NP, [in the park]PP. A system outputs [The boy]NP, [ate]VP, [the cake]NP, [in the park]NP. Compute labelled and unlabelled precision, recall and F1. Answer: predicted chunks = 4, gold chunks = 4, labelled correct = 3, so labelled P = 3/4 = 0.75, R = 3/4 = 0.75, F1 = 0.75. Unlabelled, all four boundaries match, so P = R = F1 = 1.0. The one error is a wrong label on the prepositional phrase.
chapters.trap: Scoring tokens instead of chunks, which hides boundary errors, and counting a chunk as correct when its boundary is right but its label is wrong, which only the labelled score punishes. A B- tag must open a chunk of its own type.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for phrase types and Unit 2 for POS tagging and CRF tagging.
chapters.leave: Named entity recognition detail to Unit 2, full tree building to 3.3, semantic roles to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Adding the head word to each nonterminal makes a PCFG sensitive to lexical choice, and shift-reduce parsing builds such trees left to right with a stack and a queue.
chapters.depth: Explain why a plain PCFG cannot tell 'saw the man with the telescope' from 'ate the pizza with a fork'. Define a lexicalized PCFG: each nonterminal is written with its head word and head tag, and a rule's probability is conditioned on the head words of the parent and the children. Give head percolation rules that pick the head child (S and VP take the verb, NP takes the noun, PP takes the preposition). Note the sparse-data problem and backoff from head word to head tag to nothing. Name the Collins-style parser as one family, with no numbers. Then shift-reduce parsing: a stack of built subtrees, an input queue, and the actions SHIFT, REDUCE-UNARY, REDUCE-BINARY-LEFT, REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT, FINISH; a classifier picks each action; about 2n actions for n words; greedy, so an early error propagates. Contrast it with CYK's exhaustive search.

figure.title: Shift-reduce trace, 'the boy ate the cake'
figure.aria: Six rows showing the stack after each move, growing to four cells, with the last cell of the bottom row marked as the top of the stack.

chapters.example: (a) Using S → NP VP, NP → Det N, VP → V NP, Det → the, N → boy | cake, V → ate, give the shift-reduce action sequence for 'the boy ate the cake'. (b) Choose the PP attachment in 'she saw the man with the telescope' when the head-conditioned rule NP → NP PP with head 'man' has p = 0.05 and VP → VP PP with head 'saw' has p = 0.25. Answer: (a) SHIFT the, SHIFT boy, REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as NP (the noun is the head), SHIFT ate, SHIFT the, SHIFT cake, REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as NP, REDUCE-BINARY-LEFT as VP (the verb is the head), REDUCE-BINARY-RIGHT as S, FINISH: nine moves for five words. (b) Both parses share the inner rules, so compare the differing rule: 0.25 against 0.05, so the PP attaches to the VP and the telescope is the instrument.
chapters.trap: Conditioning a rule on the head word of the parent only, which loses the lexical evidence, and treating a greedy shift-reduce decision as if it could be undone. Also forgetting that lexicalised rules multiply the number of distinct rules and need smoothing.
chapters.prereq: 3.5 for PCFGs and 3.4 for the attachment problem; 3.3 for the CYK contrast.
chapters.leave: Full neural parser architectures to Unit 6, word embeddings for lexical features to Unit 5, sense-level evidence to Unit 4.
